name: picotool
desc: Tool for interacting with RP2040/RP2350 devices and binaries
why: Talks to RP2040/RP2350 boards over USB and inspects binaries, a genuine door into low-level microcontroller internals.

brief.what_it_is: picotool is a command-line tool from Raspberry Pi for working with RP2040 and RP2350 microcontroller binaries, and for talking to the chips themselves over USB. Against a device in BOOTSEL mode it can show info, load, save, verify, erase, reboot, and read or write config and OTP memory. Against a file (ELF, UF2 or BIN) it can show binary info, convert ELF/BIN to UF2, seal or encrypt RP2350 images, build partition tables, and link binaries. Input is a board or a file; output is printed info, progress bars, or new files.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as 'a tool for working with RP2040/RP2350 binaries, and interacting with RP2040/RP2350 devices when they are in BOOTSEL mode.' It also replaces tooling that used to live in the Pico SDK, such as the elf2uf2 functionality, which the README says the uf2 convert command replaces.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes Binary Information support in the Pico SDK: compact metadata embedded in a binary that picotool can read back, from a device or a file. Device commands talk to the RP2040/RP2350 over USB while the chip is in BOOTSEL mode; from picotool 1.1 onward, the -f flag can reset a board running SDK USB stdio firmware so the command can run. Seal and encrypt add RP2350 metadata blocks, optional hashes and signatures, and OTP key material. The README does not explain the USB protocol in detail.

commands_seen.context: Shows general help; the README's synopsis block is the output of this command.
Displays all info (program, pins, build, device) from a connected device in BOOTSEL mode.
Same -a info view, but read from a UF2 file instead of a device.
Changes a binary-info config value (name) on the device, from the README's example of a configurable program setting.
Writes a UF2 file into flash on a device in BOOTSEL mode; the example output shows a progress bar.
Saves the installed program from device flash to a UF2 file.
Erases RP2350 partition 1 on the device; the README shows the before and after info output.
From the v1.1.0 release notes, not the README body: force-reboots a board with a third-party VID/PID from application firmware into BOOTSEL mode.
Creates the secp256k1 PEM signing key that picotool seal expects, as shown in the README.
Installs picotool so the Pico SDK can find it. The README says copying the binary into PATH is not enough.
From the v2.2.0 release notes: converts an OTP JSON file to a BIN file.

brief.install_notes: Pre-built executables for Windows, macOS and Linux are in the raspberrypi/pico-sdk-tools releases. Extract the archive, then set the picotool_DIR environment variable (or pass -Dpicotool_DIR to cmake, or set it in CMakeLists.txt) to point at the picotool folder. To build from source, see BUILDING.md in the repo, then run cmake --install . The README says: 'You cannot just copy the binary into your PATH, else the Pico SDK will not be able to locate it.' Hardware: the target board must be in BOOTSEL mode for most commands, or running SDK USB stdio firmware with -f or -F. Per v1.1.2 and v1.1.0 notes, Linux and macOS connection failures print a sudo suggestion. A Windows RP2040 with a custom VID/PID needs the --rp2040 flag, according to the README.
brief.standout: Picotool reads and writes RP2350 internals that most people never see: OTP fuses, secure-boot partition tables, seal and encrypt metadata, and the bootrom's block loop. The README also shows a self-decrypting binary option (encrypt --embed) and a SHA/signature path for secp256k1 keys.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as I can tell. The releases page lists 2.3.1 as Latest (dated 05 Sep; the year is not shown on the page), with 2.3.0 on 03 Jul. Release notes say the versions coincide with Pico SDK releases (2.3.1, 2.3.0, 2.2.0, and so on). I did not check the last commit date.
brief.caveats: The README was cut off at about 40,000 characters, so I did not read the otp, bdev, link, or BUILDING.md sections in detail. Device commands need a board in BOOTSEL mode, or SDK USB stdio firmware with -f. The README says the binary cannot simply be copied onto PATH, so the install goes through cmake. Signing needs secp256k1 keys specifically. I did not check the license.
